lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-9054 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/rchen
EDUCATION
Harbor State University | B.B.A. in Finance | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Lakeside Golf Club | Caddie | Metro City, USA | Aug 2025 - Present
- Caddied about 5 rounds a week, carrying bags and reading greens for members.
- Helped the pro shop run the weekend junior tournament.
Stonebridge Manufacturing | Financial Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jan 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved close efficiency by 40% by automating reconciliations and intercompany eliminations.
- Modeled the capital plan for 12 plant projects in a shared NPV template, so every request used the same discount rate and payback rules.
- Wrote the variance commentary for the monthly board pack, explaining each line more than 5% off budget.
- Valued the acquisition target by discounting its free cash flow to equity at the company's weighted average cost of capital.
- Reported a 45% group EBITDA margin by adding the EBITDA margins of the three business units.
- Built the rolling 18-month cash-flow forecast for a USD 600M manufacturer, keeping monthly forecast error under 4% and letting treasury pay down USD 40M of revolver debt early.
Crescent Bank | Credit Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Dec 2022
- Underwrote 60 small-business loans worth USD 45M, and none of the approved loans defaulted in their first two years.
- Reviewed 3 years of declined applications; my findings changed two ratio thresholds and raised approvals from 41% to 48% with no rise in early defaults.
- Writes the covenant-monitoring checklist for the portfolio, cutting missed covenant tests from 7 to 1 a year.
- Built a spreading template for borrower financials that cut each credit memo from 6 hours to 3.
PROJECTS
Regional Utility Valuation | Independent Project | Excel | Nov 2024 - Present
- Valued a listed regional utility with a 10-year DCF and a comparable-company check, landing within 6% of the market price.
- Tested the valuation's sensitivity: a 1-point change in the discount rate moved the share value from USD 52 to USD 44.
- Shared the model and a two-page note with the university investment club, which used it in its spring pitch.
Student Investment Fund | Analyst, Team of 6 | Excel | Sep 2018 - May 2019
- Supported the FP&A team with financial reporting and analysis.
- Rebuilt the fund's performance report to show returns against its benchmark, which the committee used at every meeting.
- Built an 18-month cash forecast for a USD 600M business, holding error to about 4% and freeing USD 40M to repay debt early.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Bloomberg Terminal
Methods: financial modeling, DCF valuation, forecasting, credit analysis

items.says: The Stonebridge and Student Investment Fund bullets present closely duplicative cash-forecast achievements under different entries.
items.because: Both describe an 18-month forecast, about 4% error, and USD 40M of early debt repayment, making it unclear which role the work belongs to.

items.says: Education appears before the post-graduate finance experience.
items.because: A reader sees the degree before the more recent finance work.

items.says: The caddie-duty bullet gives no result or member benefit.
items.because: A reader has little evidence of the value of the work.

items.says: The tournament bullet does not say what you did.
items.because: “Helped” leaves your specific contribution and responsibility unclear.

items.says: The tournament bullet gives no event result.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the tournament went well.

items.says: The tournament bullet should come before the caddie-duty bullet.
The caddie entry gives routine duties too much space for their finance relevance.
items.because: It shows tasks such as carrying bags and supporting a tournament, but no result relevant to the roles being pursued.

items.says: “Close efficiency by 40%” does not identify the measure or its baseline.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the gain refers to close duration, labor, or another measure.

items.says: The repeated “by” makes the result and method awkward to scan.
The template’s standardization is explained at length.
items.because: “So every request used the same” takes a long route to describe common rules.

items.says: The variance-commentary bullet describes a deliverable but not its effect.
Free cash flow to equity is discounted at the wrong rate.
items.because: It is discounted at the cost of equity; WACC is used for free cash flow to the firm.

items.says: The acquisition-valuation bullet does not state its output or what it informed.
Adding unit EBITDA margins does not calculate a group EBITDA margin.
items.because: Group margin is total group EBITDA divided by total group revenue.

items.says: The reported group margin has no stated effect or use.
The monthly forecast-error figure does not state what it was measured against.
items.because: Without a comparison basis, the under-4% claim is difficult to assess.

items.says: The USD 40M debt-paydown result comes late and is stated indirectly.
items.because: The long setup delays the clearest business outcome, and “letting treasury pay down” makes it less direct.

items.says: The zero-default result does not say how many of the 60 loans were approved.
items.because: Without that denominator, a reader cannot tell how much of the underwriting work the result covers.

items.says: The zero-default clause is wordier than needed.
The thresholds and approval result are buried behind first-person attribution.
items.because: “My findings” spends words on attribution, and “my” should not appear in a résumé bullet.

items.says: The declined-application result should lead the entry.
items.because: It shows a concrete threshold change and higher approvals without a rise in early defaults.

items.says: “Writes” is the wrong tense for a role that ended in December 2022.
items.because: It makes the checklist work sound ongoing, unlike the other completed Crescent Bank work.

items.says: “For the portfolio” is vague to readers outside the team.
The template bullet does not say what feature reduced credit-memo work.
The sensitivity bullet does not specify the discount rate’s direction or starting value.
items.because: A reader cannot tell which scenario produced each share value or whether “1-point” means a percentage point or a percent.

items.says: “Which used it” is ambiguous about what the club used.
The FP&A bullet does not identify a specific report or analysis.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what you produced.

items.says: “Supported the FP&A team with” frames the work as assistance.
items.because: It does not name your own work.

items.says: The FP&A bullet gives no result or value.
items.because: A reader cannot tell what value the work had.

items.says: The committee-use result should come before the report explanation.
items.because: Leading with that result would make the bullet’s value easier to spot.

items.says: “Which” could refer to the benchmark or the report.
The forecast-error figure does not state what it was measured against.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether it compares forecast cash with actual cash or uses another basis.

items.says: The Student Investment Fund entry is less focused because it pairs the benchmark-report work with a generic FP&A line and a duplicative forecast result.
items.because: Those lines make the older student project feel less useful beside the later finance roles.
